target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, productivity, accessibility, health, and workplace safety
objection: Those benefits do not settle the issue because AI’s real-world use is commonly accompanied by systemic harms—economic harm from automation and wage pressure, weaker critical thinking from outsourcing work and learning, biased outcomes that repeat racism, and privacy/surveillance risks—so the net effect is not good for society.

target: AG2’s assumption that the harms of AI are typically systemic, unavoidable, and cannot be meaningfully reduced
objection: That assumption is too strong because the harms are often deployment-dependent rather than inherent to AI. Economic, educational, discrimination, and privacy harms can be mitigated through reskilling, tutoring-style use, auditing/human review, and privacy-preserving design, so the claim that AI is generally net-negative is undermined.

target: AG1’s claim that AI harms are not inherently severe enough to outweigh benefits because they can be managed by deployment choices
objection: AI’s actual causal pattern in practice still produces net harms that often outweigh convenience and productivity gains: automation weakens labor demand and bargaining power, AI use reduces reasoning practice, biased data leads to discriminatory outcomes, and large-scale data collection creates privacy and surveillance risks.

target: AG2’s claim that the harms are systemic and recurrent and therefore outweigh AI’s benefits
objection: That conclusion depends on the assumption that AI is deployed mainly as replacement technology and that harms are unavoidable. In reality, AI can augment workers, support learning as a tutor, be audited for bias, and be constrained with privacy protections, so the ‘net harms reliably dominate benefits’ premise is contestable.

target: AG1’s response that AI can be governed so that its harms do not dominate its benefits
objection: Even if some good deployments exist, the typical real-world pattern remains harmful: AI often automates or deskills routine labor, weakens independent reasoning when people use it for answers and drafts, reproduces bias from historical data, and increases privacy and surveillance risks. Those recurring harms mean the benefits do not reliably improve society overall.

target: AG2’s economic-harm argument that AI typically replaces labor and harms workers
objection: That argument assumes AI is usually deployed as full automation rather than as augmentation. In many settings AI supports human work—retrieval, drafting, triage, planning, and decision support—raising productivity without necessarily eliminating jobs and creating new roles around supervising and improving AI-enabled processes.

target: AG1’s economic argument that AI often augments work and can be managed through transition policies
objection: AI commonly automates or restructures routine work in ways that still reduce labor demand and concentrate bargaining power in platform owners’ hands, so job insecurity and wage pressure remain the dominant economic effect despite possible new tasks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are inevitably recurring and cannot be brought below the benefit level
objection: That claim overstates the problem: bias can be reduced with curation, audits, transparency, and human review; privacy risk can be lowered through data minimization and privacy-preserving techniques; learning can be improved by tutoring-style use; and economic insecurity can be reduced through retraining and careful deployment. Therefore the harms are not inherently unavoidable.

target: AG1’s suggestion that contestability, auditing, and transparency can make AI’s opacity problem manageable
objection: The target’s mitigation picture is too optimistic because AI is typically deployed in ways that ordinary people and affected businesses cannot meaningfully audit or contest. As a result, outsourcing judgment, discriminatory outputs, privacy invasion, and economic dependency remain persistent harms.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity makes discrimination, privacy violations, and economic lock-in persistent and uncorrectable
objection: Opacity is not a necessary feature of AI deployment. High-impact systems can be documented, logged, tested for bias, reviewed by humans, and governed with privacy controls and portability standards, so the harms tied to black-box deployment are mitigable rather than inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that auditing and contestability are realistically achievable for AI systems in practice
objection: That is structurally too optimistic because vendors usually withhold the internals needed for meaningful auditing, fairness tests are incomplete without full data access, privacy controls do not prevent unchallengeable inference, and economic incentives discourage transparency. So the mitigation strategy does not realistically solve the problem.

target: AG2’s claim that AI systems are typically un-auditable black boxes and therefore harmful
objection: Auditability and contestability depend on design and governance, not on AI itself. Systems can be made contestable through documentation, traceable logs, third-party testing, human appeal channels, and privacy engineering, which weakens the claim that opacity makes AI net-harmful by default.

target: AG1’s claim that trade secrets, privacy limits, and legal constraints still allow meaningful AI auditing and recourse
objection: In practice, those constraints make meaningful contestability unlikely: proprietary secrecy blocks substantive audit, privacy/security limits prevent full investigation, and human review at scale is too costly, so recourse is too narrow and delayed to matter for most users.

target: AG2’s claim that proprietary internals and privacy limits prevent meaningful AI contestability
objection: Meaningful contestability can still be achieved without full access to model weights or personal data. Auditors can test behavior against standard suites, use privacy-preserving verification methods, and rely on scalable recourse mechanisms such as monitoring, rollbacks, and targeted review for high-impact cases.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous monitoring, versioning, and rollback make AI contestable despite changing models and contexts
objection: Those measures do not reliably solve the problem because audits become stale as systems and users change, harms can arise between checks, rollback is not the same as contestability for the person already harmed, and many privacy or discrimination effects only appear in narrow contexts that aggregate monitoring misses.

target: AG2’s claim that time-varying systems make meaningful contestability structurally impossible
objection: Contestability can be built into AI operations through versioned change control, continuous slice-aware monitoring, scalable dispute channels, and rapid remediation. Changes do not make audit and recourse impossible; they just require dynamic monitoring and traceability tied to the active configuration.

target: AG1’s claim that near-real-time attribution, monitoring, and recourse can reliably make AI contestable in ordinary deployments
objection: That assumption is weak because outputs depend on dynamic prompts, routing, tools, and workflows; monitoring requires detailed logs that privacy rules limit; scalable recourse is costly and therefore uncommon; and firms often cannot provide intelligible causal explanations because of trade secrets and liability concerns. So reliable contestability is more an exception than the norm.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s time dependence and changing contexts make contestability unreliable
objection: Even with changing systems, contestability can be made reliable by logging versioned configurations, continuously monitoring slice-level performance, and providing practical remediation channels. Those measures make outputs attributable and correctable enough that AI’s benefits are not defeated by opacity or drift.
